title: Mudgala turns down heaven
hook: a poor sage is offered a chariot to heaven, asks one question, and says no
carry: heaven isn't the goal; freedom is
tomorrow: a king waits one song, and ages pass

segments.voice: Yesterday: indriya-jaya, and your line: master the senses by offering them. Today something harder to master: a reward.

In the Mahabharata, Vyasa tells Yudhishthira about a sage named Mudgala, who is poor on purpose. He lives by gleaning, picking up the grain left in the fields after harvest, and every two weeks he cooks what he's gathered and feeds whoever comes to his door. Then the famously short-tempered sage Durvasa starts showing up, again and again, eating every last grain and smearing the leftovers on himself. Mudgala goes hungry, and never once gets angry. So heaven sends a chariot for him. A divine messenger at the door: get in.
screen: `A SAGE WHO LIVES ON GLEANINGS.` → `DURVASA EATS IT ALL.` → `A CHARIOT FROM HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Mudgala doesn't get in. First he asks: what's heaven like, and what's wrong with it? The messenger is honest. Heaven is lovely: no hunger, no age, music, fine company. But there you only enjoy what you've already earned; you can't do any new good. You see others shining brighter than you. And when your merit runs out, you fall. So Mudgala sends the chariot away and turns to meditation, toward a place with no grief and no falling, and the story says he reached it. Here's the Hindu teaching, plainly. Heaven, svarga, is real, but it isn't the goal. It's a reward, and rewards run out. Krishna says it in the Gita: people enjoy the wide world of heaven, and when their merit is spent, they come back. The goal is moksha, freedom, which doesn't run out. Patanjali says it in yoga's terms. Sutra 3.49: full discernment brings knowing everything. Sutra 3.50: let go even of that, and freedom comes. Sutra 3.51: when those in high places invite you, don't cling and don't be proud, or the old trouble comes back. The classical commentary acts it out: gods arrive with chariots and an elixir against age, and the yogi says no. Notice the danger is the good stuff. Nobody needs a warning against misery. It's why Prahlada, offered any boon he liked, said that serving God for a reward makes you a trader, not a devotee. A Hindu can be glad of good things, a prize, praise, a raise, and still say: that isn't the point.
screen: `MUDGALA ASKS: WHAT'S WRONG WITH HEAVEN?` · `MERIT RUNS OUT. YOU FALL.` · `SVARGA IS A STOP. MOKSHA IS THE GOAL.` · `3.51: NO CLINGING, NO PRIDE.` · then, large: `HEAVEN ISN'T THE GOAL; FREEDOM IS.`

segments.voice: Rest on the breath until something pleasant invites you away: a daydream, a plan, a drowsy warmth. Treat it like Mudgala's chariot. Notice it, thank it, don't get in. If you pray, let a name of God be how you come back: Ram, Krishna, Om namah Shivaya. If you don't, just come back to the breath. And if a little pride follows at having stayed, send that chariot away too.
Omniscience. Knowing everything, which Patanjali says comes from full discernment, and which he says to set down too, the way Mudgala set down heaven.
Your line: heaven isn't the goal; freedom is. Mudgala sent the chariot away. Rest well.

howItsDone: Hindus pray and work for good things, but the tradition teaches that heaven (svarga) is a reward that runs out and moksha is the goal; devotees remember saints like Prahlada, who were offered boons and asked for nothing but God.

fork.setup: a divine messenger offers you heaven for all your good deeds. what would Mudgala ask first?
fork.reveal: he asked about heaven's faults: merit runs out and you fall. so he chose moksha, which doesn't. sutra 3.51 adds: say no without clinging and without pride.

original.note: Sanskrit mokṣa: release, freedom; the goal Mudgala chose over svarga, heaven.

chat.says: world religions unit and i'm doing hinduism for my slides. Sam asks 'do hindus believe in heaven?' umm... do we??
options: yes, svarga. but it's a stop, not the goal. merit runs out. the goal is moksha.
yes, and getting into heaven is the whole point of being Hindu.
no, Hindus don't believe in anything after death.
chat.meaning: Mudgala asked what was wrong with heaven: merit runs out and you fall. Hindus call heaven svarga, and the real goal is moksha, freedom.

tie.story: Mudgala asked the messenger what was wrong with heaven, heard that merit runs out, and sent the chariot away.

svarga.meaning: heaven: a world of reward that lasts only as long as merit
